pages.summary: The one-sample or paired t-test: is the mean m (0 unless given)?
body: Tests whether normal data could have the mean `m`, from their sample mean and standard deviation. Given two samples of the same length, it tests the differences x - y (a paired test). `h` is 1 when the test rejects the mean at the level alpha (5%), `p` is the p-value, `ci` the confidence interval of the mean, and `stats` holds the t statistic, its degrees of freedom and the standard deviation. A matrix is tested column by column.
syntax: Is the mean of `x - y` 0 (paired data)?
With the p-value, interval and statistics; another level, or a one-sided test.

examples.title: A sample against a mean
examples.output:
h =

     1

p =

    0.0083

ci =

    5.1662    5.7838

stats = 

  struct with fields:

    tstat: 3.6374
       df: 7
       sd: 0.3694

pages.summary: The two-sample t-test: do two samples have the same mean?
body: Compares the means of two independent normal samples. By default the variances are taken to be equal; `'Vartype', 'unequal'` gives Welch's test, which does not. `ci` is the interval of mean(x) - mean(y).
syntax: [h, p, ci, stats] = ttest2(x, y, 'Alpha', alpha, 'Tail', tail, 'Vartype', 'equal' | 'unequal')
With the p-value, interval and statistics, and the options.

pages.summary: The z-test: is the mean m, for data whose standard deviation sigma is known?
body: Like the t-test, with the standard deviation known instead of estimated, so the normal distribution gives the p-value.
syntax: [h, p, ci, zval] = ztest(x, m, sigma, 'Alpha', alpha, 'Tail', tail)
With the p-value, interval and z statistic.

examples.title: A process with a known spread

pages.summary: Tests of variances: is the variance of normal data v, and do two normal samples have the same variance?
body: `vartest` uses the chi-square distribution of the sample variance; `vartest2` the F distribution of the ratio of two variances. Both depend on the data being normal.
syntax: [h, p, ci, stats] = vartest(x, v, 'Alpha', alpha, 'Tail', tail)
With the p-value, the interval of the variance and the statistic.
[h, p, ci, stats] = vartest2(x, y, 'Alpha', alpha, 'Tail', tail)
With the p-value and the interval of var(x)/var(y).

examples.title: A variance, and two

pages.summary: A test of equal variances in several groups.
body: Bartlett's test by default (for normal data); Levene's and the Brown-Forsythe test are less sensitive to departures from normality. The groups are the columns of a matrix, or the values of a vector by a grouping variable. A summary of the groups is shown unless `'Display'` is `'off'`.
syntax: The columns of `X` as the groups.

examples.title: Three groups, two tests
examples.code:
rng default
X = [normrnd(0, 1, 30, 1), normrnd(0, 1, 30, 1), normrnd(0, 2, 30, 1)];
p = vartestn(X, 'Display', 'off')
p2 = vartestn(X, 'TestType', 'BrownForsythe', 'Display', 'off')

pages.summary: Tests of a median: the sign test and Wilcoxon's signed rank test.
body: Both ask whether the median is `m` (0 unless given), or for paired data whether the median of x - y is 0, without assuming normal data. The sign test counts the values above and below; the signed rank test also uses how far they lie, and is more powerful for symmetric data. The p-value comes first, then `h`.
syntax: With `h`, the statistics and options (and the same for `signtest`).

examples.title: Paired data
examples.output:
p =

    0.0469

h =

     1

stats = 

  struct with fields:

    signedrank: 26.5000

pages.summary: The Wilcoxon rank sum test (Mann-Whitney U): do two samples come from distributions with the same median?
body: Ranks all the values together and asks whether one sample's ranks are higher than chance would give: a test of two independent samples without assuming normal data. Exact for small samples, a normal approximation otherwise.
syntax: [p, h, stats] = ranksum(x, y, 'Alpha', alpha, 'Tail', tail, 'Method', 'exact' | 'approximate')

examples.title: Two small samples
examples.output:
p =

    0.0087

h =

     1

stats = 

  struct with fields:

    ranksum: 16

pages.summary: Kolmogorov-Smirnov tests: do data come from a given continuous distribution, and do two samples come from the same one?
body: The statistic is the largest distance between distribution functions: the sample's and the given one (the standard normal unless given), or the two samples'. The given distribution's parameters must not be estimated from the same data (for that, `lillietest`).
syntax: [h, p, ksstat, cv] = kstest(x, 'CDF', pd, 'Alpha', alpha, 'Tail', tail)
[h, p, ks2stat] = kstest2(x1, x2, 'Alpha', alpha, 'Tail', tail)

examples.title: Normal, and not
examples.code:
rng default
x = randn(100, 1);
[h, p] = kstest(x)
[h2, p2] = kstest(exprnd(1, 100, 1), 'CDF', makedist('Normal', 'mu', 1, 'sigma', 1))

pages.summary: The Lilliefors test: are the data normal (or exponential, or extreme value), with the parameters estimated from them?
body: The Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic against the normal distribution with the sample's own mean and standard deviation, with the critical values that estimating them requires.
syntax: With the p-value, statistic and critical value; another family.

examples.title: Normal and skewed data
examples.code:
rng default
[h, p] = lillietest(normrnd(5, 2, 60, 1))
[h, p] = lillietest(exprnd(2, 60, 1))

pages.summary: The Jarque-Bera test of normality, from the sample's skewness and kurtosis.
body: Normal data have skewness 0 and kurtosis 3; the statistic measures how far the sample's are from these.
syntax: With the p-value, statistic and critical value.

examples.title: Normal and heavy-tailed data
examples.code:
rng default
[h, p] = jbtest(randn(200, 1))
[h, p] = jbtest(trnd(2, 200, 1))

pages.summary: The Anderson-Darling test: do the data come from a family of distributions, or from one distribution?
body: Like the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test, but weighting the tails more, so it is more sensitive to departures there. With a family's name the parameters are estimated from the data; with a distribution object they are known.
syntax: [h, p, adstat, cv] = adtest(x, 'Distribution', 'norm' | 'exp' | 'ev' | 'logn' | 'weibull' | pd, 'Alpha', alpha)
Another family, or a distribution object.

examples.title: Lognormal data tested as normal and as lognormal
examples.code:
rng default
x = lognrnd(0, 0.6, 100, 1);
[h1, p1] = adtest(x)
[h2, p2] = adtest(x, 'Distribution', 'logn')

pages.summary: The chi-square goodness-of-fit test, on the data counted in bins.
body: Compares the counts in bins with the counts a distribution expects. Without a distribution the data are tested for normality, the mean and standard deviation estimated from them; bins expected to hold fewer than 5 values join their neighbours. `stats` has the statistic, its degrees of freedom, the bins and the observed and expected counts.
syntax: [h, p, stats] = chi2gof(x, 'CDF', pd, 'NBins', n, 'Edges', edges, 'Alpha', alpha)
Against a distribution, with bins of your own.
Counts given with their expected values, a bin centred on each value of `c`.

examples.title: Is a die fair?
examples.intro: 120 rolls, counted by face, against 20 each.

pages.summary: The runs test: do the values above and below a reference (their median unless given) come in random order?
body: A run is a stretch of values on one side of the reference. Too few runs mean values cluster (a trend or a cycle); too many mean they alternate. Values equal to the reference are left out.
syntax: With the p-value and the counts of runs.

examples.title: Random order, and a trend
examples.code:
rng default
[h, p] = runstest(randn(50, 1))
[h, p, stats] = runstest((1:50)' + 5*randn(50, 1))
examples.output:

p =

h =

p =

   1.1434e-04

stats =

    nruns: 12
       n1: 25
       n0: 25
        z: -3.8579

pages.summary: One-way analysis of variance: do several groups have the same mean?
body: Splits the variation of the data into the part between the groups' means and the part within the groups, and tests their ratio with the F distribution. The groups are the columns of a matrix, or the values of a vector by group. The table is shown in the Command Window and the groups' box plots in a figure, unless the last input is `'off'`; `stats` goes to `multcompare` to see which groups differ.
syntax: The columns of `X` as the groups.
The table and statistics, nothing shown.

examples.title: Three groups, the table and the box plots

pages.summary: Two-way analysis of variance of a balanced layout: the columns are one factor, the rows (in blocks of reps) the other.
body: Tests the column factor, the row factor and, with more than one replicate per cell (`reps`), their interaction. The p-values come in that order.
syntax: `reps` rows per level of the row factor.
The table and statistics, nothing shown.

examples.title: Two factors with two replicates
examples.intro: Columns: three fertilizers; rows: two soils, two plots each.

pages.summary: The Kruskal-Wallis test: do several groups come from distributions with the same median?
body: The one-way analysis of variance of ranks, for groups whose data may not be normal. The statistic is corrected for ties and tested with the chi-square distribution. Shown as a table and box plots unless the last input is `'off'`.
syntax: The columns of `X` as the groups.

examples.title: Three skewed groups

pages.summary: Friedman's test: do the columns differ, the rows (blocks) taken out?
body: The two-way analysis of variance of ranks within blocks: each row (a judge, a subject, a day) ranks the columns (the treatments), and the test asks whether some columns rank higher throughout.

pages.summary: Which pairs of groups differ, after anova1, kruskalwallis or friedman.
body: Each row of the result compares two groups: their numbers, the interval of the difference (lower end, estimate, upper end) and the p-value, adjusted for the number of comparisons (Tukey-Kramer by default). The figure shows each group's estimate with an interval: groups whose intervals do not overlap differ.
syntax: [c, m, h, gnames] = multcompare(stats, 'Alpha', alpha, 'CType', type, 'Display', 'off')
With the groups' means and names; another adjustment; no figure.

examples.title: After a one-way analysis of variance

pages.summary: A table of counts by two or more grouping variables, with the chi-square test of their independence.
body: `tbl(i, j)` counts the observations in group i of the first variable and group j of the second. The chi-square statistic and its p-value test whether the two are independent; `labels` names the groups.
syntax: With the test and the groups' names.

    {'no'}     {'no'}

pages.summary: Fisher's exact test of independence in a 2-by-2 table of counts.
body: Exact, so it suits small counts where the chi-square test's approximation fails. `stats` has the odds ratio and its confidence interval.
syntax: Are the rows and columns independent?
With the p-value and the odds ratio.
